1.Kelibia Fort
A Greek settlement, then a Carthaginian stronghold, rebuilt into the square Byzantine citadel that still crowns this 150m headland, with the uninterrupted Mediterranean view its ramparts are famous for.

2.Kerkouane Archaeological Site
A Phoenician town abandoned during the First Punic War around 250 BC and left untouched ever since, its house foundations, dye workshops and bathtubs the clearest surviving picture of how a Punic city actually lived.

1.Bardo National Museum
A 19th-century Husainid palace turned museum, its halls given over almost entirely to the largest assembled collection of Roman mosaics anywhere in the world, lifted whole from villas across Tunisia.

A UNESCO-listed old city whose 8th-century street plan survives block for block, its souks, some 700 monuments and the Zitouna Mosque packed inside walls a visitor can still cross end to end on foot.

Day 4
From Hotel: 1h 38min → Great Mosque of Kairouan
1.Great Mosque of Kairouan
Founded in 670 AD and rebuilt in its present form by the Aghlabids, the oldest mosque in North Africa and the template its own vast courtyard, striped arcades and squat minaret set for every Maghrebi mosque after it.
Read more

24 min · 6 min → Aghlabid Basins
2.Aghlabid Basins
Built between 860 and 862 to supply a city with no river nearby, a settling basin feeding a 128m-wide main reservoir fed by a 36km aqueduct — the most important hydraulic engineering the medieval Muslim world left standing.

Open 24/7
~30 min

3.Zawiya of Sidi Sahib
Known as the Mosque of the Barber for the companion of the Prophet buried here with three hairs from his beard, a 17th-century shrine, madrasa and mausoleum wrapped in Andalusian zellij tilework and carved plaster.

1.Amphitheatre of El Jem
Raised around 238 AD in what was then Thysdrus, the third-largest amphitheatre the Romans ever built and the best-preserved anywhere outside Italy, its arena, tiers and underground animal galleries all still open to walk through.

Local Tastes
Brik à l'oeuf
A thin malsouka pastry folded around a whole egg, parsley and sometimes tuna or minced meat, then deep-fried until the sheet shatters and the yolk stays runny inside.
Restaurant Dalili · Rooh El Medina
Tunisian Mint Tea with Pine Nuts
Strong green tea poured over sugar and fresh mint, finished with a scatter of toasted pine nuts floating on top — the standard after-meal drink across every café in the country.
Cafe Sidi Bou Hdid
Harissa
A chili paste built from dried Nabeul-region peppers, garlic, caraway and olive oil, spooned onto nearly everything and sold in small jars in every Tunisian market and supermarket.
Marché Central
Food Delivery
Glovo
Foreign number: accepted — the sign-up form takes any country code, but the SMS code can be slow or fail to arrive on some foreign carriers; a local SIM improves reliability.
The only delivery platform with real coverage in the Nabeul-Hammamet area, partnering with around seven restaurants near the main tourist strip; the menu and restaurant list thin out fast once you move away from Route Touristique.
glovoapp.com
Getting Around
inDrive
Foreign number: accepted — sign-up verifies by SMS or WhatsApp through Twilio's global delivery network, which reaches most foreign carriers reliably.
The only ride-hailing app with a real presence in Hammamet since Bolt's recent exit from Tunisia; riders and drivers negotiate the fare directly in the app, so expect to counter-offer once or twice, and waits run longer than in Tunis.

Worth Knowing

Hammamet is a beach base, not a museum city — the real sightseeing happens on day trips

None of the international hotel chains that anchor most GuideMyDays picks have a property here: Marriott, Hilton and Hyatt's closest Tunisia footholds are in Tunis, Sousse and Monastir, and even second-tier Radisson Blu sits several kilometres from the old town. Every hotel in this guide is either independent or a European resort brand, which is simply what the Hammamet market offers.

Kerkouane, on Day 2, is unusual among Mediterranean ruins for what did not happen to it: abandoned during the First Punic War around 250 BC, it was never resettled or rebuilt by the Romans, so its house plans and dye-workshops survive as genuinely Punic rather than a Roman city built on Punic foundations.

The historic core of Hammamet — the Kasbah and Medina — is small enough to see on foot in half a day, which is exactly why this guide pairs it with Pupput's Roman ruins rather than padding Day 1 with a fourth in-town stop that does not exist.

El Jem's amphitheatre, saved for the last day here, sits on the same Tunis-Sousse-Sfax railway line as Hammamet's own station — but reaching it means changing trains at Bir Bou Regba, since Hammamet itself is only on the shorter branch line to Tunis and Nabeul.
